questions.q: Why does this lesson say Cascade Outfitters' warehouse integration can tolerate a staleness window of hours, unlike the ERP and financial-system case studies in Lessons 1-2?
options: Because the consumer is a batch-refreshed analytics dashboard, not a live user screen or a compliance-sensitive balance, so a short, bounded delay has no real cost
Because data warehouses are technically incapable of receiving real-time data
Because Salesforce does not allow any analytics integration to run more than once a day
Because Cascade Outfitters has no analytics team
questions.explain: The acceptable staleness window is a property of the consumer, not the technology. A dashboard refreshed a few times a day genuinely doesn't need sub-second data, which is why this integration can use a cheaper, eventually-consistent design than Lessons 1-2's operational integrations.

questions.q: What specific gap does a scheduled delta sync (querying by LastModifiedDate) have that this lesson says Change Data Capture closes?
options: Delta sync costs more API capacity than a full extract
A record created, updated, and deleted again entirely between two scheduled sync runs can be missed, because nothing matching the query remains by the time it runs
Delta sync can only run once per calendar year
Change Data Capture requires the warehouse to poll Salesforce instead of the other way around
questions.explain: A scheduled delta query only sees whatever state a record is in at query time. A record that cycles through create, update, and delete entirely between two runs leaves nothing for that later query to find, so it's silently missed -- the exact gap CDC closes by reacting to each change as it happens.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a full extract approach doesn't scale for Cascade Outfitters' warehouse feed?
options: A full extract is actually the cheapest possible approach at any org size
Re-exporting every row on every run wastes API capacity and warehouse load on records that mostly didn't change, and the job grows slower as the org grows
Full extracts are not technically possible against Salesforce
A full extract is required by Salesforce's terms of service for any analytics use case
questions.explain: Re-extracting the full dataset every run re-processes records that didn't change at all, which wastes capacity and load without benefit, and gets worse every month as the org's data volume grows -- unlike delta sync or CDC, which only move what actually changed.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does "eventual consistency" guarantee, and how is it framed for this case study?
options: That the warehouse will reflect a given Salesforce change soon, without a fixed per-event deadline -- framed as the deliberately correct design for this consumer, not a weaker compromise
That the warehouse will always be perfectly in sync with Salesforce within one second
That the warehouse will never reflect a Salesforce change until a human manually approves it
That eventual consistency is only acceptable for test environments, never production analytics
questions.explain: Eventual consistency promises the change will show up soon without a fixed per-event deadline. The lesson frames this as the deliberately correct tradeoff for a dashboard consumer that doesn't need stronger guarantees, not a lesser design forced by limitations.

questions.q: Beyond choosing CDC, what does this lesson say a warehouse feed design still needs to address?
options: Nothing further -- CDC alone fully solves the integration with no other design work needed

A way to detect subscriber backlog, a periodic reconciliation check against Salesforce, and an explicit plan for what happens if a subscriber outage outlasts Salesforce's change-event retention window
A requirement that all warehouse queries run synchronously against live Salesforce data
A rule that the warehouse may never store more than one day of historical data
questions.explain: A CDC feed is not fire-and-forget: the design still needs backlog detection, periodic reconciliation to catch silent drift, and an explicit answer for what happens if a subscriber is down longer than the retained change-event window, so an outage doesn't quietly become permanent data loss.
